Host Kernel or KVM Hypervisor Vulnerability Exploitation — Since all VMs share the same host kernel in KVM-based virtualisation, a vulnerability in the host kernel or KVM hypervisor exploited from within the VM could allow an attacker to affect the entire system, compromise other VMs, or take down the host. Flaws in KVM/QEMU leveraging the host kernel for operation can have widespread impacts.

Improper VM Isolation Allowing Inter-VM Interference — All VMs on a given host share the same host kernel (see the host-kernel trust zone), and the guest-userspace-to-host-kernel trust boundary in this model has no access control or authentication methods defined. If the VMM's network, filesystem-sharing, or other inter-VM communication configuration is not correctly hardened, a workload in one VM could exploit this shared-kernel, uncontrolled-boundary combination to affect other VMs on the same host. A malicious or flawed guest OS could engage in activities that disrupt the host or other guests.

virtio-blk / virtio-scsi Backend Exploit from Guest — The virtio-blk and virtio-scsi backends run within the VMM process (ring3 userspace) by default. A malicious container workload could craft malformed virtio ring descriptors or block requests to exploit vulnerabilities in the VMM storage backend, potentially gaining host userspace access. vhost-based back-ends for QEMU are available but not recommended due to the higher kernel-space exposure they introduce.

QEMU virtio-blk/scsi Completion Information Leak — A malicious workload can trigger vulnerable virtio-blk or virtio-scsi completion paths that return more data than was initialized by the backend, leaking host-side VMM memory to the guest. CVE-2024-8612 documents this class in QEMU virtio-scsi and virtio-blk completion handling: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whq8-5442-qhw7.

virtiofsd File Escape via Symlink or Filesystem Object — The virtiofsd daemon processes guest filesystem requests and opens files on behalf of the guest. A malicious workload could craft symlinks or filesystem objects that trick virtiofsd into accessing files outside the shared directory tree, leading to host filesystem exposure or tampering. DAX support (where the guest accesses the host page cache directly) amplifies this risk and is disabled by default.

virtiofsd seccomp Sandbox Bypass — virtiofsd sandboxes itself with seccomp(2) to prevent ptrace(2) and other attack vectors after gaining control of the process. A zero-day seccomp filter bypass or misconfiguration could allow an attacker who has compromised virtiofsd to break out of the daemon sandbox and interact with the host at root privilege.

vhost Kernel Backend Exploitation — vhost-based device backends (vhost-net for QEMU virtio-net, vhost_vsock for QEMU vsock) run within the host kernel space. An exploit targeting a vhost kernel module directly grants kernel-level privileges with no additional userspace boundary to cross, representing a higher-risk attack surface than VMM-embedded or vhost-user backends.

Host vhost Virtio Ring Descriptor Denial of Service — A malicious guest can submit malformed host-side virtio ring descriptors to vhost-based backends and trigger kernel resource exhaustion or crashes. CVE-2023-5158 documents a Linux vhost/vringh flaw where a zero-length descriptor can cause guest-to-host denial of service: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-5158.

QEMU virtio-net Buffer Handling Information Leak — When Kata uses a QEMU virtio-net backend path, a malicious guest can combine negotiated virtio-net features with crafted transmit activity to reach vulnerable VMM buffer handling and leak process memory. CVE-2023-6693 documents a QEMU virtio-net stack buffer issue that can expose process memory on the wire: https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=2023-6693.

VFIO DMA Attack Accessing Host Physical Memory — When a device is passed through to a VM via VFIO, it has direct access to host physical memory via DMA. A compromised VM could use its assigned device to read or write memory outside of its allocated space, potentially accessing credentials, secrets, or data from the host kernel or other VMs, or corrupting host state.

VFIO IOMMU Isolation Bypass or Reduced Granularity — VFIO relies on IOMMU isolation and correct group ownership to contain DMA from passthrough devices. A malicious workload with an assigned device can still reach host memory if IOMMU protection is disabled, misconfigured, reduced by PCIe topology, or weakened by sub-page DMA exposure. Linux VFIO documentation describes reduced IOMMU isolation granularity, and EuroSys 2021 research demonstrates DMA code-injection risks even with IOMMU page-granularity protection: https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/vfio.html and https://borispis.github.io/publications/2021-iommu-vuln.

VFIO Device Isolation Failure Causing Inter-VM Interference — If a VM can affect the operation of a physically passed-through device in a way that impacts other VMs or the host system, it could lead to security breaches, system instability, or denial of service. Improper configuration of VFIO group or user permissions can expose the system to this risk.

VFIO Device Resource Starvation — Improperly managed, a VM with direct access to hardware resources through VFIO could monopolize those resources, leading to performance degradation or denial of service for other VMs or the host system.

Improper VFIO Configuration and Device Management — Human errors in VFIO configuration, group ownership, user permissions, monitoring, or lifecycle management can expose devices to the wrong VM or leave unsafe device state unhandled, leading to security lapses beyond the initial device assignment.

VFIO Device Passthrough Privilege Escalation — If a VM with VFIO access is compromised, it could use exposed I/O device capabilities that are not adequately controlled or monitored to gain higher privileges than intended.

VFIO Inter-VM Interference and Side-Channel Leakage — Even with device assignment, an attacker VM may infer sensitive information from the behavior of a shared physical device or shared host resources such as cache, creating inter-VM information disclosure without direct memory access.
ACPI-Based VM Escape — A sophisticated attacker could exploit ACPI functionality to achieve a VM escape, where malicious code in the VM breaks out to the host system or other VMs.

ACPI Request Handling Vulnerability in Hypervisor — In virtualized environments, the hypervisor manages ACPI calls for VMs. Vulnerabilities in ACPI request handling could lead to escalated privileges or other security breaches affecting the host or neighboring VMs.

Firmware Attack Through Virtualized ACPI — Firmware-based attacks, including those targeting ACPI in virtualized systems, can be persistent and difficult to detect. In a virtualized environment such compromise may affect the host and all VMs running on it.

ACPI Power Management Manipulation for Resource Starvation — ACPI functionality could be exploited to manipulate power management features, causing denial of service through resource starvation. For example, an attacker could force a VM into a low-power state, degrading its performance or availability.

Compromised VM Alters Host ACPI Settings — If a VM is compromised, it might be used to alter ACPI settings on the host, affecting all VMs on that host and causing impacts ranging from performance degradation to system instability.

VM Resource Exhaustion Denial of Service — A VM could consume excessive shared resources such as CPU, memory, or I/O bandwidth in KVM/QEMU or other VMM setups, leading to resource starvation for other VMs or the host. This could be due to misconfiguration, a runaway process, or a deliberate denial of service attack from a compromised VM.

Malicious or Flawed Guest Operating System Disrupting Host or Other Guests — A guest operating system that is maliciously designed or has serious flaws could engage in activities that disrupt the normal operation of the host or other guests. For QEMU specifically, the virtio-net backend defaults to vhost-net, a host kernel module (see virtio-net-backend); aggressive or malformed network activity from such a guest reaches host kernel code directly rather than being contained in host userspace, unlike the in-VMM backends used by Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor, and Dragonball.

Cross-VM Speculative Execution Side-Channel — A malicious workload sharing CPU resources with other VMs can exploit speculative execution side channels to infer sensitive data from privileged kernel or hypervisor memory, applications, or other virtual machines. Red Hat's Spectre/Meltdown advisory describes this cross-VM exposure for CVE-2017-5715 and CVE-2017-5754 class issues: https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/speculativeexecution.

VFIO Passthrough Device Firmware Vulnerability — Devices attached via VFIO rely on their firmware, which can have vulnerabilities. A compromised device firmware could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the host or to disrupt the system. Such firmware-level compromises can be persistent and difficult to detect or remediate.

Vulnerability in VFIO Kernel Modules, Drivers, or Management Tools — Like any software, the components of VFIO — including the kernel modules, device drivers, and management tools — can have vulnerabilities that might be exploited by an attacker to compromise the security of the system and gain control of the host.

Supply Chain Compromise of ACPI Firmware — ACPI firmware used in virtualised environments could be compromised during the supply chain process, leading to persistent vulnerabilities that affect all VMs running on the hardware. Such attacks are difficult to detect and could not only compromise the host system but all VMs running on it.
